title: Easter baskets
hook: Polish Catholics bring food to be blessed on Holy Saturday

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve days: wise men crossing the living room one shelf at a time. Your line was keep the feast. What did you carry a day further? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

Holy Saturday morning, in a Polish parish. The church is strangely quiet; there's no Mass during the day. But the aisle fills anyway, with families carrying wicker baskets lined with white cloth and tucked with sprigs of green. Inside: a few painted eggs, a piece of sausage, a heel of bread, a little salt, a spoonful of horseradish, and often a small lamb made of sugar or butter. The baskets go in rows on long tables. A priest comes down the line with holy water and a prayer, and the water spatters the cloth, the eggs, and a few delighted children. Today's word is that basket, and the meal waiting for it.
screen: `A QUIET CHURCH ON HOLY SATURDAY.` → `BASKETS LINED WITH WHITE CLOTH.` → `HOLY WATER ON THE EGGS.`

segments.voice: First, the day. Holy Saturday is the Church at the tomb. The Roman Missal describes it as a day when the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, and there's no Mass until the Easter Vigil after dark. Into that quiet, families bring their food. It's a small act of hope on a day of waiting: setting out the Easter meal before Easter has come. Second, the name. In Polish it's święconka, the blessed food, and the word is used for the basket and for the custom. The contents vary from family to family, and people give them meanings as they pack: eggs for new life, bread for Christ the bread of life, salt for what preserves and gives taste, the lamb for the Lamb of God. Those meanings are tradition, passed on at kitchen tables, not rules. Third, the blessing. The Church has blessings for food at Easter, and a priest or deacon asks God to bless the food and the people who will share it. It's the same instinct as grace before meals, written large: the whole Easter table is lifted up before anyone eats. Last, the meal. The basket goes home and waits. On Easter morning, families sit down and share its food at breakfast, often starting by passing a blessed egg around the table. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus stands on a beach at dawn beside a fire with fish on it, and says to his tired friends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come, and dine." Risen from the tomb, in this story, he makes breakfast.
screen: `THE CHURCH WAITS AT THE TOMB.` · `ŚWIĘCONKA, THE BLESSED FOOD.` · `THE WHOLE TABLE IS BLESSED.` · `BREAKFAST ON EASTER MORNING.` · then, large: `COME, AND DINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to bless your Easter meal, or any meal you'll share. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a table you'll sit at soon. Who will be there? What will be on it? See one dish clearly. Then see it covered with a white cloth, waiting, while you wait too. Notice what it's like to prepare a feast before the reason for it has arrived. If you pray, you can ask God to bless that food and the people who'll eat it. If you don't, simply give thanks for them, one by one. The bell holds the time.
Easter baskets. Baskets of Easter food, eggs, bread, salt and more, brought to church on Holy Saturday to be blessed and shared at Easter breakfast. In Polish, święconka. Today's word.

Your line: święconka. Today, before the next meal you share, pause long enough for a blessing or a thank-you over the whole table, and start by passing something around. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: On Holy Saturday, Polish Catholic families, in Poland and in Polish parishes elsewhere, bring baskets of Easter food to church to be blessed by a priest or deacon, then share the food at breakfast on Easter morning.

fork.setup: your basket has just been sprinkled with holy water on Holy Saturday. when does the custom say you eat it?
options: right away, on the church steps.
after the Easter octave is over.
fork.reveal: it goes home and waits through the night. on Easter morning the family shares it, often starting by passing a blessed egg.

original.note: Polish, the blessed food: both the basket and the Holy Saturday custom.

trapdoor: what you thought: an Easter basket full of candy.
what it means: a basket of the Easter meal, blessed in church on Holy Saturday and shared at breakfast on Easter morning.
what a scholar hears: the blessing falls on the day the Church waits at the tomb with no daytime Mass, so the feast is prepared before it arrives.

sources.ref: Book of Blessings, blessing of food for Easter

notes: Roman Missal, Holy Saturday paraphrased: the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, and the sacrifice of the Mass is not celebrated until the Easter Vigil. Confirm.
Book of Blessings: confirm that a blessing of food for Easter (for first meal of Easter) exists and may be led by a priest or deacon.
Basket contents and their meanings are presented as varying family tradition, with 'often' for the lamb. Confirm the list is fair to Polish practice.
Passing a blessed egg at Easter breakfast is described with 'often'; the custom of sharing an egg with wishes (dzielenie się jajkiem) may deserve naming by a Keeper.
John 21 is not the first resurrection appearance; the teach says 'in this story' to avoid implying it is.
